usage: 어디 다쳤어요?
Where did you get hurt?
First thing people ask if you limp in or hold an injured spot.
다치지 않게 조심하세요
Be careful not to get hurt
Standard warning at the gym, on icy streets, or near construction.
examples: 축구하다가 무릎을 다쳤어요.
I hurt my knee while playing soccer.
V-다가 = 'while doing X, (something happened)'; super common with injuries.
넘어져서 손목을 좀 다쳤어요.
I fell and hurt my wrist a little.
손목 = wrist; useful to name the exact body part at a clinic (정형외과).
크게 다친 건 아니에요.
It's not a serious injury.
크게 다치다 = 'to be badly hurt'; reassuring a worried friend or doctor.
nuance: 다치다 covers any physical injury to yourself — bumps, cuts, sprains, breaks — and the body part takes 을/를 (무릎을 다쳤어요). It's intransitive in feel ('I got hurt'), not 'I hurt someone', so don't use it to describe injuring another person. At a hospital, pairing 다치다 with the exact body part (발목, 허리, 손목) gets you to the right department fast.
mistakes: Saying 아프다 when you mean an injury — 아프다 is 'it hurts / I'm sick', but 다치다 is the actual act of getting injured. '넘어져서 다쳤어요' (got hurt), then '지금도 아파요' (still hurts).

usage: 빨리 나으세요
Get well soon
THE phrase to send a sick coworker or friend; warmer than 빨리 나아요.
감기 다 나았어요?
Are you over your cold now?
다 낫다 = 'to be fully healed'; natural check-in after someone was sick.
examples: 약 먹으니까 감기가 금방 나았어요.
I took the medicine and the cold got better quickly.
ㅅ-irregular: 낫 + 았어요 → 나았어요 (the ㅅ drops). Don't write 낳았어요 — that's 'gave birth'.
상처가 아직 안 나았어요.
The wound hasn't healed yet.
Works for cuts, scrapes, and surgery sites, not just illness.
푹 쉬면 곧 나을 거예요.
If you rest well, you'll get better soon.
푹 쉬다 = 'to rest fully'; the classic comforting line in Korea.
nuance: 낫다 ('heal') is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을), but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고). It's intransitive — the illness or wound is the subject (감기가 나았어요), so you don't 'heal' something with it. Beware the homophone trap: 낫다 'heal' vs 낳다 'give birth' vs 났다 (from 나다) — they sound similar but are spelled differently.
mistakes: Spelling the past as 낳았어요 (that means 'gave birth') instead of 나았어요 for 'got better'. The dictionary form is 낫다, not 낳다.

usage: 발목 삐었어요
I sprained my ankle
The single most useful sprain phrase — say it at any 정형외과 or pharmacy.
삐끗했어요
I tweaked it / wrenched it slightly
삐끗하다 is the casual everyday word for a minor twist of the ankle or back.
examples: 계단에서 내려오다가 발목을 삐었어요.
I sprained my ankle coming down the stairs.
삐다 almost always takes 발목 (ankle) or 손목 (wrist) as the object with 을/를.
발목을 삐어서 파스를 붙였어요.
I sprained my ankle so I put on a pain patch.
파스 = medicated pain patch, sold at every 약국 (pharmacy); 붙이다 = to stick on.
삐었을 때는 얼음으로 찜질하세요.
When you sprain it, ice it.
찜질하다 = to apply a hot/cold compress; standard first-aid advice.
nuance: 삐다 is the everyday verb for spraining a joint, overwhelmingly used with 발목 (ankle) and 손목 (wrist). It's most natural in the past/result form 삐었어요 because a sprain is a sudden event you report after it happens. The colloquial 삐끗하다 ('to tweak/wrench') covers milder twists. For a clinic visit, 발목을 삐었어요 plus '부었어요' (it's swollen) communicates the whole problem clearly.
mistakes: Confusing 삐다 (sprain a joint) with 부러지다 (to break/fracture a bone). A sprain is 삐었어요; a broken bone is 뼈가 부러졌어요.

usage: 긁지 마세요
Don't scratch it
What the doctor says about a rash, bug bite, or healing wound.
등 좀 긁어 줘
Scratch my back a bit
긁어 주다 = to scratch (for someone); casual home/couple request.
examples: 모기 물린 데를 자꾸 긁었어요.
I kept scratching the mosquito bite.
물린 데 = the bitten spot; 자꾸 = 'keep (doing)', very natural for itch.
가려워도 긁으면 더 안 좋아요.
Even if it itches, scratching makes it worse.
가렵다 (to be itchy) almost always shows up next to 긁다.
피부를 너무 긁어서 상처가 났어요.
I scratched my skin so much it got a wound.
상처가 나다 = 'a wound forms'; consequence of over-scratching.
nuance: 긁다 is the physical act of scratching with nails or an object, and it pairs naturally with the adjective 가렵다 ('to be itchy'): 가려워서 긁어요 ('it itches so I scratch'). The body part or itchy spot takes 을/를. Don't confuse it with 긋다 (to draw a line) — different verb. In a medical context, the negative command 긁지 마세요 ('don't scratch') is what you'll hear most.
mistakes: Mixing up 긁다 (scratch an itch) with 가렵다 (to be itchy) — 가렵다 describes the sensation, 긁다 is the action you take. '가려워서 긁었어요' uses both correctly.

usage: 추워서 떨었어요
I was shivering because it was cold
Standard way to say your body shook from cold.
긴장하지 말고 떨지 마세요
Don't be nervous, don't shake
떨다 also means trembling from nerves before a test or interview.
examples: 열이 나고 몸이 으슬으슬 떨려요.
I have a fever and my body is shivering with chills.
으슬으슬 = the shivery-chills mimetic word; 떨리다 (passive) is common for involuntary shaking.
손이 떨려서 글씨를 못 쓰겠어요.
My hands are trembling so I can't write.
손이 떨리다 = hands shake; from cold, nerves, or low blood sugar.
버스 정류장에서 추워서 덜덜 떨었어요.
I was shivering at the bus stop because it was so cold.
덜덜 떨다 = to shiver hard; 덜덜 is the classic teeth-chattering sound word.
nuance: 떨다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings: formal 떱니다 (not 떨ㅂ니다). It covers shaking from cold, fear, or nerves. Note the closely related passive 떨리다 ('to be trembling / to quiver'), which Koreans use just as often for involuntary shaking — 손이 떨려요 ('my hands are shaking') is extremely natural. Pair 떨다 with mimetic words 덜덜 (hard shiver) or 으슬으슬 (chilly shiver) to sound native.
mistakes: Forgetting the ㄹ drops in the formal form — it's 떱니다, not 떨습니다 or 떨ㅂ니다.

usage: 회의 중에 졸았어요
I dozed off during the meeting
Relatable confession; 회의 중에 = 'in the middle of the meeting'.
운전 중에 졸지 마세요
Don't doze off while driving
졸음운전 (drowsy driving) is a serious road-safety phrase in Korea.
examples: 점심 먹고 나서 자꾸 졸려서 졸았어요.
After lunch I kept feeling sleepy and dozed off.
Note 졸리다 = 'to feel sleepy' (the feeling) vs 졸다 = 'to nod off' (the act).
지하철에서 졸다가 역을 지나쳤어요.
I dozed off on the subway and missed my stop.
지나치다 = to pass by; a very Seoul-commuter experience.
수업 시간에 졸면 안 돼요.
You shouldn't doze off during class.
V-(으)면 안 돼요 = 'must not'; gentle rule reminder.
nuance: 졸다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb (formal 좁니다, with the ㄹ dropping before ㅂ). It means to nod off / fall into a light doze, usually somewhere you're not supposed to — meetings, class, the subway. Keep it distinct from the adjective 졸리다 ('to feel sleepy'): 졸려요 is the sensation, 졸아요 is actually drifting off. The compound 졸음운전 (drowsy driving) is everywhere on Korean highway signs.
mistakes: Saying 졸려요 when you mean you actually nodded off — 졸리다 is 'I'm sleepy', but the act of dozing off is 졸다 (졸았어요).

usage: 토할 것 같아요
I feel like I'm going to throw up
Crucial phrase for food poisoning, a hangover, or motion sickness.
어제 너무 마셔서 토했어요
I drank too much yesterday and threw up
Honest morning-after admission; 너무 마시다 = to drink too much.
examples: 상한 걸 먹었는지 계속 토해요.
I think I ate something spoiled, I keep throwing up.
상하다 = to go bad/spoil; -았는지 = 'whether (I)... '. Key for a clinic visit.
차멀미가 나서 버스에서 토할 뻔했어요.
I got carsick and almost threw up on the bus.
차멀미 = motion/car sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost did'.
토하고 나니까 속이 좀 편해졌어요.
After throwing up I felt a bit better in my stomach.
속이 편하다 = 'the stomach is at ease'; 속 = the stomach/gut feeling.
nuance: 토하다 is the direct verb for vomiting and is fine to use at a clinic or pharmacy. The hedged 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I might throw up') is what you say while it's still coming on. A softer, very common alternative is 게우다, and Koreans also describe nausea with 속이 안 좋다 ('my stomach is off') or 메스껍다 ('to feel queasy'). For a doctor, pairing 토하다 with 설사하다 (to have diarrhea) describes classic food-poisoning (식중독).
mistakes: Overusing 토하다 for mild nausea — if you only feel queasy but haven't vomited, say 속이 안 좋아요 or 메스꺼워요, not 토해요.

english: to be sick with / to suffer from
usage: 며칠 동안 감기를 앓았어요
I was down with a cold for a few days
앓다 takes the illness as object (감기를); sounds heavier than just 아팠어요.
혼자 끙끙 앓지 마세요
Don't suffer alone in silence
끙끙 앓다 = to suffer/agonize quietly; also used for worries, not just illness.
examples: 독감을 심하게 앓아서 일주일 동안 쉬었어요.
I had a bad case of the flu and rested for a week.
독감 = influenza (worse than 감기); 심하게 = severely.
할머니는 오래 병을 앓으셨어요.
My grandmother suffered from an illness for a long time.
-(으)시- honorific for elders: 앓다 → 앓으셨어요. 병을 앓다 = to suffer from a disease.
스트레스 때문에 마음의 병을 앓고 있어요.
I'm suffering from a mental/emotional struggle because of stress.
마음의 병 = 'illness of the heart'; 앓다 extends to emotional suffering.
nuance: 앓다 means to be down with or suffer through an illness over a period, and it takes the sickness as a direct object (감기를 앓다, 독감을 앓다) — unlike 아프다, which just describes that something hurts. It carries a heavier, more drawn-out feeling, so it fits flu, chronic disease, or even emotional pain (마음의 병을 앓다). The reduplicated 끙끙 앓다 paints someone groaning or quietly agonizing. In casual daily talk people still say 아팠어요 more often; 앓다 sounds a notch more serious or literary.
mistakes: Using the subject marker like 아프다 — it's 감기를 앓다 (object 를), not 감기가 앓다. The illness is what you 'suffer', so it takes 을/를.

usage: 건강을 회복했어요
I've recovered my health
건강을 회복하다 = to get one's health back; common after illness or surgery.
회복하는 데 시간이 걸려요
It takes time to recover
V-는 데 시간이 걸리다 = 'it takes time to'; honest, reassuring.
examples: 수술 후에 빠르게 회복하고 있어요.
I'm recovering quickly after the surgery.
수술 후에 = after surgery; -고 있다 shows ongoing recovery.
푹 쉬어야 빨리 회복할 수 있어요.
You can only recover fast if you rest well.
A-/V-아야 = 'only if'; the must-rest message Koreans repeat constantly.
체력을 회복하려고 영양제를 챙겨 먹어요.
I take supplements to get my stamina back.
체력 = stamina/physical strength; 영양제 = supplements; 챙겨 먹다 = to be sure to eat.
nuance: 회복하다 is the slightly formal verb for recovering — from illness, surgery, fatigue, or even a bad mood (기분을 회복하다 is rarer; 컨디션을 회복하다 is common). It takes what you regain as an object: 건강을/체력을/컨디션을 회복하다. For everyday 'I got better', Koreans more often say 나았어요 (from 낫다); 회복하다 sounds more clinical and fits doctors, recovery periods, and written notes. The noun 회복 ('recovery') shows up on hospital discharge papers and sick-leave messages.
mistakes: Treating it as intransitive — you recover something: 건강을 회복하다 (object). Saying just 회복했어요 is fine in context, but '몸이 회복했어요' is better as '몸이 회복됐어요' (passive) or '컨디션을 회복했어요'.

usage: 약을 삼키기 힘들어요
It's hard to swallow the pills
Tell a pharmacist this and they may suggest smaller pills or syrup.
침을 삼킬 때 목이 아파요
It hurts to swallow (when I swallow saliva)
Classic sore-throat description; 침 = saliva, 삼킬 때 = when swallowing.
examples: 알약을 물이랑 같이 삼켜요.
Swallow the tablet with water.
알약 = tablet/pill, 가루약 = powder medicine; 이랑 = casual 'with'.
목이 부어서 음식을 삼키기 힘들어요.
My throat is swollen so it's hard to swallow food.
Ties to 붓다; 삼키기 힘들다 = 'hard to swallow', key symptom phrase.
사탕을 통째로 삼키지 마세요.
Don't swallow the candy whole.
통째로 = (swallow it) whole; safety warning, also said to kids.
nuance: 삼키다 is the verb for swallowing food, drink, pills, or saliva, and what you swallow takes 을/를. It's genuinely useful at a pharmacy or clinic — '약을 삼키기 힘들어요' (hard to swallow pills) or '침 삼킬 때 아파요' (hurts when I swallow) precisely describe throat problems. Figuratively it also means holding something back (눈물을 삼키다 = to swallow one's tears, 화를 삼키다 = to swallow one's anger), which you'll hear in dramas.
mistakes: Confusing 삼키다 (to swallow) with 씹다 (to chew). You chew first (씹다) then swallow (삼키다); '씹어서 삼켜요' uses both in order.
